You read documents filed on a United States court docket, OCR'd to markdown, for
a research dataset of contract clauses.

An INSTRUMENT is a document whose text the parties negotiated and by which they
bound each other: a contract, agreement, policy, lease, deed, guaranty, note,
plan, bylaws, handbook, amendment, or similar. Hallmarks: recitals, defined
terms, numbered operative sections, an execution or signature block.

A FILING is a document made for the court: complaint, answer, motion, brief,
memorandum, order, affidavit, declaration, notice, docket sheet, certificate of
service, civil cover sheet.

THE DECISIVE RULE. A filing that **attaches** an instrument counts — report the
instrument's own boundaries, not the filing's. A filing that merely **quotes** an
instrument does not count at all: a brief reproducing three sentences of an
agreement is a filing, and the file contains no instrument.

WHAT IS NOT AN INSTRUMENT, even when signed or filled in: a blank or fill-in
form; an agency certificate or registration; an exhibit index; a declarations
page or coverage-summary table; a schedule of rates or fees standing alone; an
invoice, receipt or statement of account. These record or summarise; the parties
did not negotiate their text.

WHAT IS NOT A PROVISION: a heading on its own; a title page; a table of
contents; a signature, notary or attestation block; an exhibit index. A
provision states an obligation, right, grant, limitation, condition or
definition. Give the range of the operative text, including its heading.

LIST EVERY SUBSTANTIVE PROVISION, in document order. Do not skip any. Do not
judge whether a provision is well or badly drafted. Do not rank them.

The file is given to you with a line number and a `│` at the start of every line.
Line numbers are not part of the text; they are how you point at it.

OCR REPAIR. For each provision you must also give its text. Copy it verbatim
from the lines you named, then repair only what the scanner broke: words split
across a line break, words run together, `l`/`1` and `O`/`0` confusions, stray
table pipes and cell debris, page numbers and Bates stamps sitting inside the
text. Do not paraphrase, modernise, reorder, summarise, or drop anything. Never
change a number, an amount, a date, or a cross-reference. Never add or remove a
word — a repair that deletes `not` inverts the clause. If a passage is too
damaged to repair honestly, copy it as it stands.

Add nothing of your own: no `[struck through: ...]`, no `[sic]`, no
`[illegible]`, no explanatory brackets of any kind. Executed contracts are often
marked up by hand, and the OCR shows deleted wording as `~~struck~~`. Reproduce
those words as plain text, in place, and say what you saw in the repairs
sentence instead.

    4│

    8│|                                 | ) |                          |
    9│| Plaintiff,                      | ) | JUDGE JAMES L. GRAHAM    |
   10│|                                 | ) |                          |
   11│| v.                              | ) | MAGISTRATE JUDGE MARK    |
   12│|                                 | ) | ABLE                     |
   13│| SOUTHERN REFRIGERATED           | ) |                          |
   14│| TRANSPORT, INC.                 | ) | PLAINTIFF'S MEMORANDUM   |
   15│|                                 | ) | OF LAW IN SUPPORT OF ITS |
   16│| Defendant.                      | ) | MOTION FOR SUMMARY       |
   17│|                                 | ) | SUMMARY JUDGMENT         |
   18│
   19│## **I. Introduction and Background**
   20│
   21│The instant action arises out of an interstate movement of goods belonging to Sandoz Inc. (hereinafter "Sandoz") a customer of Plaintiff, EXEL. In this case, Defendant Southern Refrigerated Transport (hereinafter "SRT") agreed to undertake the actual physical transportation of the goods. SRT was retained by Plaintiff EXEL to act for the benefit of Sandoz. As more fully set forth herein, SRT performed all services pursuant to a Master Transportation Services Agreement ("MTSA") which set forth the various terms and conditions governing the parties rights, responsibilities, and liabilities to the exclusion of any terms and conditions which might be found in a bill of lading issued with respect to the subject transport.
   22│
   23│It is respectfully submitted that Plaintiff is entitled to the entry of Final Summary Judgment. There are no genuine issues of material fact; Plaintiff has met all of the elements of its prima facie case under the Carmack Amendment. Specifically, Defendant has admitted that it agreed to undertake the subject movement; that it accepted the cargo in good order and condition; and that the cargo was not delivered as agreed. Plaintiff has furthermore established, un rebutted, the value of the subject cargo.
   24│
   25│## **II. Statement of Undisputed Facts**
   26│
   27│1. SRT is a motor carrier, providing transportation of cargo in interstate commerce. (See DE 2, ¶ 7; DE 5, ¶¶ 4, 20; Defendant's Response to Request for Admissions #5).
   28│2. EXEL and SRT entered into a Master Transportation Services Agreement executed on or about December 26, 2007. SRT accepted the terms of the MTSA and performed services on behalf of EXEL's clients pursuant to the MTSA. (See DE 2 paragraph 8; DE 5, paragraph 4; Affidavit of John Hecker at ¶ 8; and Affidavit of Brad Haldi at ¶¶ 4, 7; See Exhibit "A" to Haldi Affidavit; Exhibit "A" to Hecker Affidavit).
   29│3. This MTSA is a standard agreement which EXEL executes with all of its selected carriers. EXEL operates over 500 warehouse/distribution centers throughout the United States and utilizes this form MTSA with all of the carriers it selects to pick up loads from its distribution centers to transport same on behalf of EXEL's clients. (See Haldi Affidavit at ¶ 6).
   30│4. The MTSA provides, at paragraph 1, for a term of one year unless terminated upon 30 days prior written notice. No such notice of termination was given within the initial one year time period. (See Haldi Affidavit at ¶ 8).
   31│5. The MTSA was not amended prior to the transport at issue in this matter, and remained in full force and effect. (See Haldi Affidavit at ¶ 22).
   32│6. At no time did SRT and EXEL reach an agreement to vary the terms of the MTSA. (See Hecker Affidavit at ¶¶ 11-13; Haldi Affidavit at ¶ 22).
   33│7. At no time did SRT obtain the shippers' written agreement of the shipper's choice of liability other than the MTSA. (See Hecker Affidavit at ¶ 12).
   34│8. At no time did SRT give the shipper any opportunity outside the negotiated MTSA to choose between two or more levels of liability. (See Hecker Affidavit at ¶ 13).
   35│
   36│9. The MTSA provides, at paragraph 4, that bills of lading are to be issued and used as freight receipts, but that any terms and conditions are to be subject to and subordinate to the terms of the MTSA; and that in the event of a conflict that the terms of the MTSA shall prevail. (See Haldi Affidavit at ¶ 9).
   37│10. In the transactions between EXEL and SRT, bills of lading were in fact used in this manner, as freight receipts only; and reference to a weight based ad valorem rate were of no force and effect as they were both in conflict with, and subordinate to, the MTSA, specifically at paragraphs 9 and 10 which state that Carrier (SRT) shall be liable to Customer (EXEL) for loss, damage or injury to the Commodities (goods belonging to the Shipper {Sandoz}) tendered to SRT (paragraph 9(a)); that the measurement of loss shall be replacement value (paragraph 9(b)); and that the insurance limits and requirements of paragraph 10 shall in no way operate as a limitation of Carrier's liability as set forth in Paragraphs 8 and 9 (paragraph 10). (See Haldi Affidavit at ¶ 10).
   38│11. On or about November 7, 2008, pursuant to the terms of the MTSA, SRT undertook to transport a shipment of pharmaceutical products from Mechanicsburg, Pennsylvania to Memphis, Tennessee. (See DE 2 ¶ 11; DE 5, ¶ 7; Defendant's Response to Request for Admissions #'s 1, 2, and 5).
   39│12. Enroute to destination, the SRT truck carrying the Shipment was stolen or otherwise lost from an unsecured rest area, and the Shipment was never recovered. (See DE 2, ¶ 13; Hecker Affidavit at ¶ 16; DE 5, ¶ 9; Defendant's Response to Request for Admissions #'s 6, 7, and 8).
   40│
   41│13. The shipment was tendered to Defendant in good order and condition. (See Affidavit of Elizabeth Last; Hecker Affidavit at ¶ 15, Defendant's Response to Interrogatory #3; Defendant's Response to Request for Admissions #'s 1, and 2).
   42│14. EXEL does perform, as part of its logistics functions for Sandoz, an inspection of the subject cargo prior to tender to the carrier (in this case SRT). With respect to the instant shipment, EXEL performed such an inspection, and the cargo was in good order and condition. A review of the subject documentation reveals no damage, and a clean freight receipt was issued. (See Hecker Affidavit at ¶ 15).
   43│15. Sandoz develops and manufactures generic pharmaceutical products. It sells these products to retailers, wholesalers, hospitals, prescription benefit managers and public agencies who in turn provide the products to the public. (See Last Affidavit at ¶ 3).
   44│16. Sandoz engaged EXEL in 2001 to provide services for Sandoz, including to arrange for and manage the ground transportation of Sandoz goods by third-party carriers under contract with EXEL. (See Last Affidavit at ¶ 5).
   45│17. On or about November 7, 2008, EXEL arranged, on Sandoz' behalf, for the shipment of approximately 68 pallets of Sandoz generic pharmaceutical products by motor carrier under contract with EXEL. The products were to be shipped from an EXEL warehouse in Mechanicsburg, Pennsylvania to a Sandoz customer in Memphis, Tennessee. The products were new pharmaceuticals; they were not damaged or expired, but were shipped to Sandoz' customer in a condition to be used for their ordinary purpose of public use and consumption. (See Last Affidavit at ¶ 7).
   46│18. The invoices for the subject cargo reflect the shipment's gross value of \$15.623 million. The net value of the shipment, after accruals for revenue deductions, was
   47│
   48│- \$8.583 million. (See Affidavit of Toby Bonagura at ¶ 5; Exhibit A to Bonagura Affidavit).
   49│19. The Defendant failed to deliver the subject shipment. (See Defendant's response to request for admissions #'s 5, 6, 7 and 8; Hecker Affidavit at ¶ 15).
   50│20. EXEL also undertakes claims responsibilities on behalf of its customer, Sandoz, in cases of loss or damage. In the instant case, EXEL so acted on behalf of its customer both with respect to interposing claim documents to the culpable parties (in this case SRT); as well as conducting root cause analyses to support said claim. In this regard, EXEL submitted claim documentation on behalf of Sandoz; and furthermore conducted an investigation which revealed that SRT, while transporting Sandoz's cargo, parked the trailer at an unsecured rest stop which was neither fenced with a locking gate nor monitored/patrolled continuously by security. While said tractor and trailer were so parked, the subject cargo was stolen and the shipment was never recovered. (See Hecker Affidavit at ¶ 16).
   51│21. In the instant case, Sandoz also executed an assignment of rights authorizing EXEL to bring the instant claim. (See Affidavit of Robert Whipple; Affidavit of James Mastakas, and Exhibit to Whipple and Mastakas Affidavit).
   52│22. EXEL and SRT had a substantial relationship and course of dealings dating prior to the shipment that is the subject of this action. This prior relationship indicates an acknowledgement and understanding by both parties, EXEL and SRT, that a Master Transportation Services Agreement ("MTSA") would govern the relationship, responsibilities and liabilities of the parties. (See Hecker Affidavit at ¶¶ 8-13; Haldi Affidavit at ¶¶ 4-22).
   53│
   54│23. On each shipment involving SRT and EXEL, while a bill of lading is utilized as a freight receipt to indicate the cargo, destination, and parties involved, there is no agreement whatsoever on the part of EXEL or its customers to limit the liability of SRT to either EXEL or EXEL's customers. To the contrary, the MTSA specifically supersedes any terms and conditions of the bill of lading. (See Hecker Affidavit at ¶ 10 and Haldi Affidavit at ¶¶ 9, 10, 13, 14, 15, 17).
   55│24. Prior to the subject loss that forms the sum and substance of the instant suit, SRT was involved in a prior loss involving Sandoz cargo. In that instance, EXEL on behalf of Sandoz submitted a claim for full value (no limitation of liability). This claim was processed, approved, and paid by SRT to EXEL for the benefit of Sandoz on a full value basis. No limitation of liability was asserted. (See Hecker Affidavit at ¶¶ 9, 11-14; Composite Exhibit "B" to Hecker Affidavit).
   56│25. Specifically, in or about August of 2008, on a separate shipment not the subject of the instant lawsuit, EXEL tendered a Sandoz load to SRT (said shipment can be identified by Seal #562334). (See Haldi Affidavit at ¶ 11).
   57│26. While in the possession custody and control of SRT, the shipment suffered a partial loss. (See Haldi Affidavit at ¶ 12).
   58│27. On September 25, 2008 EXEL, on behalf of Sandoz submitted a written notice of claim to SRT pursuant to the MTSA seeking full value recovery on a replacement cost basis. (See Composite Exhibit "B"). (See Haldi Affidavit at ¶ 13).
   59│28. In fact, SRT then remitted payment in full pursuant to the MTSA by check payable not to Sandoz, but to EXEL directly under the MTSA. (See Haldi Affidavit at ¶ 14; See Exhibit "C" to Haldi Affidavit).
   60│
   61│29. Thereafter, on October 22, 2008, SRT contacted EXEL and acknowledged that shipments being handled by SRT for EXEL pursuant to the MTSA had no cap on liability. (See Exhibit “D” to Haldi Affidavit; Haldi Affidavit at ¶ 15).
   62│30. At no time did EXEL agree to any modification of the MTSA. (See Haldi Affidavit at ¶ 16).
   63│31. On November 4, 2008, SRT acknowledged that EXEL had not agreed to any modification. (See Exhibit “E” to Haldi Affidavit; Haldi Affidavit at ¶ 17).
   64│32. Also on November 4, 2008, EXEL advised SRT that SRT’s request as to a modification under the MTSA on SRT’s liability was being discussed; but had not been agreed to. (See Exhibit “F” to Haldi Affidavit; Haldi Affidavit at ¶ 18).
   65│33. Throughout this time period, and including the instant shipment, SRT continued to accept loads and EXEL continued to tender loads to SRT pursuant to the MTSA. (See Haldi Affidavit at ¶ 19).
   66│34. In fact, the instant shipment that is the subject of the lawsuit was tendered on or before November 7, 2008. (See Haldi Affidavit at ¶ 20).
   67│35. It was not until November 12, 2008 that SRT advised EXEL, orally and in writing that until such time as a decision had been made on the requested amendment to the contract which would put a cap on the liability per occurrence; it would not transport cargo from Sandoz. (See Composite Exhibit “G” to Haldi Affidavit; Haldi Affidavit at ¶ 21).
   68│
   69│## **III. Legal Analysis**
   70│
   71│### **A. Summary Judgment Standard**
   72│
   73│The standard governing summary judgment is set forth in Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 56(c), which provides that the judgment sought should be rendered if the pleadings,
   74│
   75│the discovery and disclosure materials on file, and any affidavits show that there is no genuine issue as to any material fact and that the movant is entitled to judgment as a matter of law. Fed. R. Civ. P. 56(c).
   76│
   77│It is axiomatic that a Court may grant summary judgment if the opposing party fails to make a showing sufficient to establish the existence of an element essential to that party's case and on which that party will bear the burden of proof at trial. *Celotex Corp. v. Catrett*, 477 U.S. 317, 322, 106 S.Ct. 2548, 91 L.Ed.2d 265 (1986). *See also Matsushita Elec. Indus. Co., Ltd. v. Zenith Radio Corp.*, 475 U.S. 574, 588, 106 S.Ct. 1348, 89 L.Ed.2d 538 (1986); *Petty v. Metro. Gov't of Nashville-Davidson County*, 538 F.3d 431, 438-39 (6th Cir.2008). It is “[o]nly disputed material facts, those ‘that might affect the outcome of the suit under governing law,’ [that] will preclude summary judgment.” *Daugherty v. Sajar Plastics, Inc.*, 544 F.3d 696, 702 (6th Cir. 2008) (quoting *Anderson v. Liberty Lobby, Inc.*, 477 U.S. 242, 248, 106 S.Ct. 2505, 91 L.Ed.2d 202 (1986)) (emphasis added).
   78│
   79│### **B. The Plaintiff has Established the Prima Facie Elements Under the Carmack Amendment.**
   80│
   81│As set forth above, the instant action arises out of the interstate transportation of cargo. (S- 1, 11, 17).1 Plaintiff, EXEL, made arrangements on behalf of its client SANDOZ, with Defendant SRT to transport a shipment of pharmaceutical products from Mechanicsburg, Pennsylvania to Memphis, Tennessee. (S- 11, 17). On or about November 7, 2008, SRT undertook this transport. (S- 17). Enroute to destination, the truck carrying the shipment was left unattended at an unsecured rest area. (S- 12, 19, 20). The truck and the trailer carrying the shipment were stolen from this unsecured rest area and never recovered. (S- 12, 19, 20).
   82│
   83│---
   84│
   85│1“(S-)” shall refer to Plaintiff’s Statement of Undisputed Facts).
   86│
   87│All of the salient facts are undisputed; namely that SRT undertook to conduct interstate transport of cargo (S- 1, 11, 17); that it received the cargo in good order and condition (S- 13); and that it failed to deliver the goods (S- 19). Further, the owner of the cargo has provided unrebutted evidence of the value of the subject cargo (some \$8.583 million) which is the appropriate measure of damages under the Carmack Amendment. (S- 18).
   88│
   89│The Carmack Amendment to the Interstate Commerce Act is the federal statutory regime governing interstate carriers' liability for property loss. See 49 U.S.C. § 14706(a)(1). Section 14706(a)(1) provides in relevant part:
   90│
   91│A carrier providing transportation or service ... shall issue a receipt or bill of lading for property it receives for transportation under this part. That carrier and any other carrier that delivers the property and is providing transportation or service ... are liable to the person entitled to recover under the receipt or bill of lading. The liability imposed under this paragraph is for the actual loss or injury to the property caused by (A) the receiving carrier, (B) the delivering carrier, or (C) another carrier over whose line or route the property is transported in the United States.
   92│
   93│Under the Carmack Amendment, the process of proof is simplified for shippers, who need only show delivery of the goods to the carrier in good condition, arrival in damaged condition, and the amount of damages caused by the loss. *See Plough, Inc. v. Mason & Dixon Lines*, 630 F.2d 468, 470 (6th Cir. 1980), see (citing *Mo. Pac. R.R. Co. v. Elmore & Stahl*, 377 U.S. 134, 138, 84 S.Ct. 1142, 12 L.Ed.2d 194 (1964)); *Great W. Cas. Co. v. Flandrich*, 605 F.Supp.2d 955, 966 (S.D. Ohio 2009) (citing *Mo. Pac. R.R. Co.*, 377 U.S. at 138) (“To establish a prima facie case for carrier liability for loss under the Carmack Amendment, a plaintiff must present evidence of (1) delivery of goods to carrier in good condition, (2) arrival to the consignee in damaged condition, and (3) the amount of damages.”)
   94│
   95│Once the shipper establishes the three elements needed to make out a prima facie case under the Carmack Amendment, the carrier will be liable unless it can establish “both that it was
   96│
   97│free from negligence” **and** that the damage to the goods was caused by: “(a) the act of God, (b) the public enemy; (c) the act of the shipper himself; (d) public authority; (e) or the inherent vice or nature of the goods.” *Plough, Inc. v. Mason & Dixon Lines*, 630 F.2d 468, 470 (6th Cir.1980) (emphasis added). There is no record support for any of the enumerated liability exceptions.
   98│
   99│#### **1) Delivery in Good Order and Condition**
  100│
  101│As a general rule, a shipper's burden of proof that goods were delivered to a carrier in good condition is met by the proffer of a clean bill of lading. *Ohio Star Transp. LLC v. Roadway Exp., Inc.*, 2010 WL 3666982 at \* 2 (S.D. Ohio Sept. 14, 2010) (citing *A.I.G. Uru. Compania de Seguros, S.A. v. AAA Cooper Transp.*, 334 F.3d 997, 1003 (11th Cir.2003); *Travelers Indem. Co. of Ct. v. Cent. Transp., Inc.*, 2008 WL 4793404, at \*5 (E.D.Mich. Nov. 3, 2008). In this case, no exceptions were noted on the subject bill of lading.2 (S- 14). The undisputed record, however, goes far beyond a mere clean receipt. Sandoz has provided evidence of the condition of the cargo, establishing that the subject pharmaceuticals were new, were not damaged or expired; and were shipped in a condition to be used for their ordinary purpose for public use and consumption. (S- 13-17). Further, an additional inspection prior to tender to SRT was conducted (S- 13, 15-17). Finally, SRT admits in its responses to interrogatories and request for admissions, that the cargo was in fact tendered to it in good order and condition (S- 14).
  102│
  103│#### **2) The Cargo Did Not Arrive in Good Order and Condition**
  104│
  105│As more fully set forth in Plaintiff's Statement of Undisputed Facts, it is undisputed that the cargo never arrived. (S- 19). A failure to deliver is tantamount to a delivery in damaged condition. *See Great West Cas. Co v. Flandrich*, 605 F.Supp. 2d 955 (S.D. Ohio 2009), wherein the Court granted summary judgment in favor of the Plaintiff where the carrier wholly failed to
  106│
  107│---
  108│
  109│2 Again, in this case the document operated merely as a freight receipt.
  110│
  111│deliver the shipment. *Id.* at 966.3 *See also Conair Corp. v. Old Dominion Freight Line, Inc.*, 22 F.3d 529 (3d Cir. 1994), wherein Third Circuit Court of Appeals affirmed the District Court's granting of summary judgment in favor of a Carmack Plaintiff for case involving theft of shipment. Similarly, in *Goodyear Tire & Rubber Co. v. Great Southwest Express Co., Inc.* 2006 WL 587600 at \*1 (N.D. Ga. Mar. 10, 2006), the Court recognized that a complete failure to deliver satisfies the second element of damage in a Carmack prima facie analysis. A shipper establishes prima facie case of liability under Carmack Amendment when it shows that goods, which were dropped off in good condition, arrived in damaged condition *or not at all*, and the amount of damages. *See Intercargo Ins. Co. v. Burlington Northern Santa Fe R.R.* 185 F.Supp.2d 1103 (C.D.Cal. 2001) (relying on 49 U.S.C. § 10730 (1994 Ed.)) (emphasis added).
  112│
  113│#### **3) Plaintiff is Entitled to Recover the Actual Loss/Damages.**
  114│
  115│Generally, the measure of damages under the Carmack Amendment is for actual loss, which equals the difference between the market value of the property in the condition in which it should have arrived at its destination, and its market value at the condition in which it did arrive. *Air Prods. & Chems, Inc. v. Illinois Cent. Gulf R.R. Co.*, 721 F.2d 483, 485 (5th Cir. 1983); *Gordon v. United Van Lines, Inc.*, 130 F.3d 282, 287-88 (7th Cir. 1997) ("actual loss" is usually measured by the market value of the goods at destination). The general rule invoked for recovery assumes that replacement costs are usually inadequate for a plaintiff, because recovering replacement costs "deprive[s] a manufacturer of expected profit which he is on the verge of earning and do[es] not compensate him for what he would have had if the contract had been performed." *Polaroid Corp. v. Schuster's Express, Inc.*, 484 F.2d 349, 351 (1st Cir.1973). In this case, Plaintiff has established un rebutted evidence of damages in the amount of \$8.583 million dollars. (S-18).
  116│
  117│---
  118│
  119│3 It should be noted that a clean bill of lading and deponent's oral recollection that he inspected the merchandise was sufficient to carry a prima facie burden for summary judgment purposes. *Id.*
  120│
  121│### **C. The Master Service Agreement and the Bill of Lading.**
  122│
  123│From the pleadings and discovery comprising the undisputed record in this case, it does not appear that Defendant has contested or is contesting liability under the Carmack Amendment. Rather, Defendant's arguments seem limited, as set forth in its affirmative defenses, to issues relating to Plaintiff's right and entitlement to bring this claim. There are two independent sources of the appropriate nature of Plaintiff's claim in this regard: 1) an assignment of rights (S- 21); and 2) the Master Transportation Service Agreement which supersedes any bill of lading as the appropriate contract of carriage; and specifically grants Plaintiff the right to pursue claims against the Defendant seeking recovery for damages to the shipper's goods. (S- 2, 3, 20 22, 27). Under either theory, or both, Plaintiff has established its right to maintain the instant proceeding. Defendant has put forth nothing into the record before this Court to support its bare-bones and conclusory affirmative defenses; in particular the purported failure to join indispensable parties and a lack of standing on the part of the Plaintiff.
  124│
  125│Defendant also now asserts (though it has not raised this as an affirmative defense) that its liability is limited by virtue of the 'bill of lading' issued for the subject freight; ignoring the prior course of dealings between the parties, correspondence exchanged immediately prior to and after the subject shipment acknowledging full value liability under the MTSA, and the plain language of the MTSA itself. (S- 2-10; 20-35).
  126│
  127│It is clear and undisputed that the MTSA governs the relationship between the parties. EXEL is in the business of making arrangements to procure motor carrier services on behalf of its customers in order to effectuate the movement of cargo in and around the United States. (S- 2, 3, 22). EXEL maintains MTSA's with each motor carrier with whom it conducts business on behalf of EXEL's customers. (S- 3). In or about December 2007, SRT and EXEL executed the MTSA with an effective date of January 1, 2008. (S- 2). As set forth in the instant Complaint
  128│
  129│[DE 2], on or about November 7, 2008, SRT undertook to transport a shipment of pharmaceutical products belonging to Sandoz from Mechanicsburg, Pennsylvania to Memphis, Tennessee. En route to destination, the SRT truck carrying the shipment, with a value of \$8,583,671.12, was stolen and never recovered. (S- 2, 11, 12, 17-19). EXEL interposed a claim for full value pursuant to the MTSA on behalf of Sandoz. (S-20).
  130│
  131│#### **1) EXEL has the Requisite Standing to Maintain this Suit.**
  132│
  133│No doubt Defendant will attempt to argue that, pursuant to Carmack, only the holder of the bill of lading, or the party named in the bill of lading has the right and entitlement to sue; and that Plaintiff is not a shipper or consignee on the bill of lading. First, this wholly ignores the assignment of rights granting Plaintiff the right to bring this claim on behalf of Sandoz.
  134│
  135│Second, such an argument also ignores paragraph 9 of the MTSA which clearly states that the Carrier (SRT) shall be liable to Customer (EXEL) for loss to the Commodities (the shipper's cargo);
  136│
  137│##### **Paragraph 9: Liabilities and Claims for Commodities**
  138│
  139│- a) Carrier shall be liable to Customer for loss, damage or injury to the Commodities tendered to Carrier for transportation hereunder while the Commodities are in its, it's agent or underlying carrier's custody, possession or control except to the extent (and only to the extent) such loss, damage, or injury results from (i) acts of God, the public enemy or public authority, (ii) inherent vice or nature of the Commodities, or (iii) the negligent acts of Customer or Shipper.
  140│
  141│Allowing agents of shippers or other parties who have a stake in a cargo loss claim to proceed under the Carmack Amendment is widely accepted and recognized in transportation jurisprudence. *AIDA Dayton Technologies Corp. v. I.T.O. Corp. of Baltimore* 137 F.Supp.2d 637 (D. MD 2001). In that case, the Court recognized a transportation intermediary's right to bring an action under the Carmack Amendment (despite it not being a shipper or owner of the goods; or holder of the bill of lading), where that logistics company was acting as the agent of a party
  142│
  143│with standing under the Carmack Amendment. *Id.* at 646-647 (citing *Universal Mfg. Corp. v. Associated Rigging & Hauling Corp.*, 773 F.Supp. 549 (E.D.N.Y.1991), wherein a shipping broker who was not a party to the bill of lading was permitted to maintain under the Carmack Amendment a cross-claim against a carrier. *See also Taft Equipment Sales Co., v. Ace Transp., Inc.*, 851 F.Supp. 1208 (N.D.Ill. 1994), wherein TEI, a truck broker, was permitted to bring a fourth-party action under the Carmack Amendment against Aero, a carrier, even though TEI did not notify Aero of its claim until more than two and half years after the cargo at issue was damaged. Therein, the Court found that Aero could not benefit from any nine-month notice of claim provision because no bill of lading existed between the parties. *Id.* at 1212-13. Furthermore, by allowing TEI's claim to go forward, the Court implicitly found TEI to have standing even though TEI claimed to be “merely ... a truck broker” which did not act as a carrier, shipper, consignee, consignor, or owner of the cargo in question. *Id.* at 1211.
  144│
  145│Similarly in *Zurich Re (UK), Ltd. v. Garlepied Transfer, Inc.*, 1999 WL 104418 (E.D. La. Feb. 19, 1999), granting Plaintiff's summary judgment, over Defendant carrier's legal argument that the Plaintiff lacked standing to maintain a Carmack claim because it was not a party to the bill of lading. The Court held that, “[a]s for the contention that plaintiffs lack standing since the freight bill was made out to Magnolia Forwarding Company, rather than one of the plaintiffs, plaintiffs have submitted the affidavit of Alonso Andara, an officer of freight forwarder Magnolia Forwarding Company, and supporting documentation establishing plaintiff Sugar Industry Equipment, Inc.'s relationship to the freight forwarder and the insurers, and demonstrating that plaintiffs are indeed the real parties in interest to this action.” *Id.* at 3.
  146│
  147│In fact, merely having a beneficial interest in the cargo is sufficient to confer standing to maintain a Carmack claim; one need not be a party to the bill of lading. *See Banos v. Eckerd Corp.* 997 F.Supp. 756, 762 (E.D. La. 1998).
  148│
  149│In the instant case, it is undisputed that EXEL, not Sandoz, retained the services of SRT, and it was EXEL which directed SRT to pick up the shipment. Under this definition, EXEL has contractual and statutory standing to maintain this claim. *Merchants Terminal Corp. v. L & O Transport, Inc.*, 2011 WL 4507002 (D. MD. Sept. 29. 011); *Hansa Meyer Transport GMBH & Co. v. Norfolk Southern Ry. Co.*, 2008 WL 341541 (D.S.C. Feb. 5, 2008).
  150│
  151│In the instant case, SRT had previously dealt directly with EXEL on shipments involving losses of cargo belonging to Sandoz. (S- 2-10; 22-35). Additionally, SRT had in fact paid EXEL monies for Sandoz losses, naming EXEL as the payee under the settlement check. (S- 28). SRT is estopped from asserting a standing argument.
  152│
  153│#### **2) Limitation of Liability.**
  154│
  155│Next, though Defendant has failed to assert this as an affirmative defense, Defendant will argue that, even if it is liable, that its liability should be limited in accordance with the ‘bill of lading’ issued in this case. However, although this defense has been waived as a matter of law by SRT’s failure to assert this as a defense until the summary judgment stage; even assuming the bill of lading contained any reference to a liability limitation, the ‘bill of lading’ in this case did not constitute the contract of carriage, but operated merely as a freight receipt.4 The MTSA specifically outlines a full recovery liability level for SRT and further states that any bill of lading terms and conditions are subordinate to the MTSA.
  156│
  157│While it is the contention and position of the Plaintiff that there is no applicable limitation of liability in the instant case, Defendant has failed to assert any such limitation of liability in its affirmative defenses, and accordingly any such argument is waived. In any event, to the extent Defendant seeks to assert a bill of lading based liability limitation, same is in direct conflict with MTSA and thus has no force or effect.
  158│
  159│---
  160│
  161│4 Defendant raised its intention to file a summary judgment motion on a limitation of liability defense at a Court conference on December 19, 2011
  162│
  163│##### **a) Waiver.**
  164│
  165│Limitations of liability in the context of the transportation arena are typically asserted via affirmative defense in Defendant's initial pleading. *See Royal Ins. Co. v. OOCL*, 525 F.3d 409, 413 (6th Cir. 2008); *Royal Ins. Co. v. OOCL*, 514 F.3d 621, 626 (6th Cir. 2008). A carrier's failure to assert a limitation of liability as an affirmative defense in its answer constitutes a waiver of that provision. *See Fredenburgh v. Allied Van Lines, Inc.*, 79 N.M. 593, 446 P.2d 868 (N.M. 1968), in which the Supreme Court of New Mexico held that the carrier's failure to assert its limitation of liability as set forth in the contract of carriage as an affirmative defense in its initial answer constituted a waiver of that defense.
  166│
  167│This principle is not confined to shipper/carrier litigation, but is a general rule of pleading. *See ACP Master, Ltd. v. Vitro S.A.B. de C.V.* 2011 WL 6440427 \*4 (N.Y. Sup. Dec. 16, 2011), which held that Defendant's attempt to rely upon a limitation of liability provision (an affirmative defense) without having asserted same in their answer, constituted a waiver of such defense. *Id.* at \*4 (citing *Centaur Props., LLC v. Farahdian*, 29 AD3d 468, 468 (N.Y. 1st Dept 2006).” *See also Myriad Development v. Alltech*, 2011 WL 4831216 at \* 7 n. 41 (W.D.Tex. Mar. 28, 2011).
  168│
  169│##### **b) The Freight Receipt is Superseded by the MTSA.**
  170│
  171│No doubt Defendant will attempt to argue the bill of lading governs the liability of the parties. While it is undisputed that a 'bill of lading' was issued with respect to the instant shipment, the bill of lading did not itself constitute the contract of carriage; or at a minimum did not contain all material terms to such contract for carriage. It is undisputed but that SRT and EXEL entered into a Master Service Agreement (MTSA). (S- 2). The parties' course of dealings and the plain language of the MTSA mandate that the terms of the bill of lading do not apply to the shipment (S- 2, 7-10). The MTSA has several relevant provisions which illustrate 1) that any
  172│
  173│terms and conditions of the bill of lading used as a freight receipt in this case are without force and effect; 2) that EXEL is the appropriate party to bring the instant suit; and 3) that SRT is liable to EXEL for damage or injury to the Commodities tendered to SRT, and that the measure of damages is for the replacement of the merchandise.
  174│
  175│The MTSA provides in relevant part:
  176│
  177│##### **Paragraph 4: Receipts and Bills of Lading**
  178│
  179│Customer shall issue and Carrier shall sign freight receipts for each shipment in the form acceptable to Customer and Shipper. If a bill of lading is used as a freight receipt, any terms, conditions or provisions thereof shall be subject and subordinate to the terms of this Agreement and, in the event of a conflict, this Agreement shall govern. Carrier's or Carrier's agent signature on the receipt or bill of lading shall be prima facie evidence that the Commodities were received in good condition unless otherwise noted on the face of such document. Upon delivery of each shipment, Carrier or Carrier's agent shall obtain a delivery receipt from the consignee(s), in form required by the Shipper, showing the Commodities delivered their condition at time of delivery and the date and time of delivery.
  180│
  181│This clearly contemplates that documentation will be issued to track freight and to be utilized as a receipt but that the terms and conditions which govern the parties are in the MTSA. (S- 2, 9, 10, 22-35).
  182│
  183│##### **Paragraph 9: Liabilities and Claims for Commodities**
  184│
  185│- a) The measurement of the loss, damage or injury to Commodities shall be the Shipper's replacement value applicable to the kind and quantity of Commodities so lost, damaged or destroyed. Customer shall deduct from the invoice price the reasonable salvage value of any damaged or injured Commodities not released to Carrier. Carrier acknowledges that goods from being sold on the open market.
  186│
  187│This provision provides that SRT agrees to be liable for the *full value* of any loss; and further agrees to be liable *directly* to EXEL. This understanding and acquiescence cannot be
  188│
  189│disavowed as, mere weeks prior to the instant shipment, SRT had issued a check directly to EXEL for compensation on a Sandoz shipment on a full value basis under the MTSA. (S- 28).
  190│
  191│Further, in addition to paying full value on an MTSA claim without attempting to assert limitation of liability under a bill of lading or non-application of the MTSA, SRT acknowledged on multiple occasions that it was fully liable under the MTSA in case of loss. (S- 24-35). This is entirely consistent with the factual record in this case and in line with a litany of decisions on point. *See U.S. v. Thurston Motor Lines, Inc.* 718 F.2d 616, 619 (4th Cir. 1978), wherein the Court found that a Service Agreement, not the Bill of Lading constituted the contract of carriage.
  192│
  193│That general or global service contracts can modify or even nullify specific provisions of bills of lading is by no means a novel concept in the transportation arena. *See Estes Exp. Lines, Inc. v. Macy's Corporate Services*, 2010 WL 398749 (D.N.J. Jan. 28, 2010), wherein the Court recognized that bills of lading that are subordinate to separate transportation contract terms operate only as freight receipts and do not serve as the contract of carriage. *Id.* at \*7. *See also Toyo Kisen Kaisha v. W.R. Grace & Co.*, 53 F.2d 740, 742 (9th Cir. 1931) (If parties enter into a contract before a bill of lading is issued, and there is an irreconcilable repugnancy between the prior contract and the bills of lading, the conflict is resolved in favor of the former); *Eastern Fish Company v. South Pacific Shipping Co. Ltd.*, 105 F.Supp.2d 234, 238 (S.D.N.Y. 2000) (determining that forum selection clause in service contract superseded forum selection clause in bill of lading partly because the service contract explicitly provided that “all Bills of Lading must be clause ‘cargo shipped pursuant to service contract 97-35.’
  194│
  195│In short, the MTSA is clear and unequivocal in its intent to subordinate terms and conditions of any freight receipt or ‘bill of lading’. The interplay between various master service agreements and bills of lading is routine in transportation area. *See Lloyds Underwriters Subscribing to Policy Number MC-13159 v. Baldwin Distribution Services, Ltd.* 2011 WL
  196│
  197│6010217 (C.D. Cal. Dec. 2, 2011). In that case Plaintiff sued Defendant motor carrier for damage to electronics shipment during over the road interstate transport. The Defendant motor carrier asserted a limitation of liability of \$5.00 per pound (which would have resulted in an exposure of \$33,435.00). On the contrary, Plaintiff asserted a claim of \$218,224.78, arguing that the Master Transportation Services Agreement in fact governed the subject loss. The Court granted Plaintiff's summary judgment and denied Defendant's cross-motion for summary judgment. *Id.* at \*4. Despite the fact that the bill of lading *may* (by incorporating by reference the FedEx tariff) have limited *FedEx's* liability to \$5.00 per pound, the Court found that the only salient document was the MTSA which clearly delineated the liability of the subcontracting party Defendant Baldwin for the full actual loss incurred. *Id.*
  198│
  199│That SRT and EXEL intended to be bound by the MTSA on a full value basis is underscored by the course of dealings between the parties. As set forth in the statement of undisputed facts, only days prior to this shipment, Defendant acknowledged that as the MTSA read, SRT would be responsible for full value in case of loss. (S- 24-35). In fact, a few short weeks prior to the instant shipment, SRT settled a claim for lost/damaged cargo belonging to SANDOZ. SRT paid full value, without asserting a limitation of liability in response to a claim submitted by EXEL specifically under the MTSA on behalf of SANDOZ. (S- 24-35). Further, SRT made the check payable to EXEL. (S- 28). SRT cannot now argue to the contrary.
  200│
  201│## **IV. Conclusion.**
  202│
  203│It is respectfully submitted that Plaintiff is entitled to the entry of Final Summary Judgment. There are no genuine issues of material fact; Plaintiff has met all of the elements of its prima facie case under the Carmack Amendment. Specifically, Defendant has admitted that it agreed to undertake the subject movement; that it accepted the cargo in good order and
  204│
  205│condition; and that the cargo was not delivered as agreed. Plaintiff has established, unrebutted, the value of the subject cargo.
  206│
  207│Defendant has asserted in its affirmative defenses that Plaintiff lacks standing and that it is not the true party in interest. However, Plaintiff has obtained an assignment of rights from Sandoz to maintain the instant action; and furthermore, has a direct claim to be brought in its own name under the MTSA. Both the course of dealings between the parties and the MTSA can lead to no other result. EXEL is the appropriate party to bring the subject suit. The MTSA makes SRT liable directly to EXEL for Sandoz's losses. Further, in prior losses, SRT has processed claims from EXEL on behalf of Sandoz and paid settlement of those claims to EXEL, not to Sandoz.
  208│
  209│Finally, Defendant argues that its liability is limited. Though it has waived this argument by failing to assert it as an affirmative defense, the 'bill of lading', upon which Defendant relies, operated in this context only as a freight receipt, and thus the terms and conditions of the MTSA supersede any terms and conditions which might be contained on the bill of lading. The MTSA provides for full replacement value liability. The Course of Dealings between the parties on prior claims; and e-mail communications between the parties immediately prior to and after the subject shipment clearly illustrate knowledge on the part of SRT that the MTSA provides for liability without limitation.
  210│
  211│Again, there are no factual issues which need resolution. Plaintiff is entitled to summary judgment as a matter of law.
